docs.text: Business case previews ¶ Five business problems, one for each department. Each case teaches a core skill and a common mistake to catch. Previews, not assignments yet These are proposed case themes. Individual files have not been released yet. We combine selected Tableau sample datasets with synthetic (made-up) teaching data. Meridian Commerce is a proposed fictional company used only for the synthetic cases. Real datasets keep their own context, units and dates. The five core cases ¶ Retail ¶ Decision: Which customer segment deserves a closer investigation? You will practise: what a row means, distinct orders, average order value, Sales and Profit, ratios, discounts, customers, trends and the limits of a returns list. Mistake to catch: treating order lines as orders. Finance ¶ Decision: Which departments need a spending review? You will practise: budget versus actual, time periods, reconciliation and whether a cost difference is favourable. Mistake to catch: repeating a monthly budget on every transaction row. Operations ¶ Decision: Where should delivery reliability improve? You will practise: promised dates, overdue open shipments, distributions, median and mean. Mistake to catch: dropping undelivered shipments from the service measure. Marketing ¶ Decision: Which campaigns need closer evaluation before budget moves? You will practise: weighted funnel rates, cost per conversion, return on ad spend and the limits of attribution. Mistake to catch: averaging percentages that have different denominators. HR ¶ Decision: How is the workforce changing, and which comparisons are fair? You will practise: historical headcount, turnover, cohorts, tenure and recruitment timelines. All employee records are synthetic. Mistake to catch: dividing past exits by the current headcount. What every case includes ¶ Stakeholder brief : the decision and why it matters Data dictionary : what each field means Metric definitions : exact formulas and scope Worked example : a guided walk-through Exercises : guided and independent practice Debugging task : find and fix a mistake Recommendation challenge : advise the stakeholder Validation checkpoints : confirm your numbers Each case also has an optional pandas connection. Instructor answers are supplied separately. Combining evidence across departments ¶ Before combining findings, explain any differences in grain, period and units. Within the synthetic company, marketing-attributed revenue is a view of the same retail revenue. Do not count it twice. Separate catalog datasets do not describe that fictional company. A good recommendation weighs trade-offs. It does not add incompatible KPIs together. Additional practice choices ¶ You will also be able to practise on topics beyond the five departments: Topic Example dataset Sports World Cup match results Technology Mobile operating-system usage (a data-quality exercise), start-up funding Government US construction spending, US home sales Other Science, education and entertainment datasets These are transfer exercises: the same process, with source-specific definitions and checks. They fit into your existing practice time or optional extensions. The five core cases remain the foundation of your portfolio. Every dataset is reviewed first A dataset appearing in a catalog does not tell us what each row means, which calculations it supports or whether it can be shared. Each lesson will give you the exact reviewed file and dictionary, or instructions to download it from the source, before you use it.

docs.text: From business question to recommendation ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision. A chart becomes trustworthy when its population, calculations and limitations are clear. We follow the same seven steps in every lesson and case. The seven steps ¶ 1. Business question ¶ Ask: Who must decide what, and by when? Keep: the decision and a one-sentence question. 2. Data understanding ¶ Ask: What does each row represent? What is missing? Keep: the grain, keys, units, data dictionary and scope. 3. Preparation ¶ Ask: What changes are needed, and could someone else repeat them? Keep: an untouched copy of the original data and a log of every change. 4. Analysis ¶ Ask: Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? Keep: the metric definition, filters and calculation. 5. Validation ¶ Ask: Do totals reconcile? Can I explain any odd values? Keep: a manual spot check, count and total checks, and edge cases. 6. Visualization ¶ Ask: Can the audience see the important comparison at a glance? Keep: a labelled chart showing the period, units and population. 7. Recommendation ¶ Ask: What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Keep: an action linked to evidence, one caveat and a follow-up measure. A worked example ¶ Why are orders falling? A manager asks: "Why are orders falling?" The data file has one row per order line , so a single order with three products takes up three rows. Counting rows would count lines , not orders. First, define what an order is, which period to look at and which orders are eligible. Then count distinct order IDs in that population. Compare the result with an order-level summary before reading anything into the trend. The same care applies elsewhere in the course: a budget repeated on every row after a join undelivered shipments left out of a service calculation campaign percentages averaged without their volumes past staff exits divided by today's headcount When a result looks wrong ¶ Work through these checks in order: Grain and keys Date filters Missing values Join or relationship behaviour Aggregation Then write down why the wrong answer was tempting and what evidence supports the corrected one. A plausible number is not a checked number Looking reasonable is not the same as being validated. Association is not causation ¶ A pattern in the data can tell you where to look . It does not prove that a discount, campaign, carrier or HR policy caused a result. When a decision depends on cause and effect, recommend a follow-up comparison or a test.

docs.text: Why data analytics matters ¶ Every organisation makes decisions. Data analytics is the discipline of making those decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and of explaining that evidence so other people act on it. Before we write any code or build any charts, this Foundations section answers a simple question: why bother? You will see how analysis has changed real outcomes, how numbers can mislead, and why the way we present evidence matters as much as the evidence itself. What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854) ¶ During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows". A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s) ¶ After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it. Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002) ¶ The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004) ¶ Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions. When big data got it wrong (public health, 2008–2015) ¶ Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation. Where you meet analytics every day ¶ Banking: a card payment is flagged as possible fraud because it does not fit your normal pattern. Streaming and shopping: recommendations are based on what similar customers watched or bought. Transport: ride-hailing prices rise when demand outstrips available drivers. Healthcare: hospitals plan staff rotas using predicted admission levels. Workplaces: HR teams track hiring time and staff turnover to spot problems early. Why presentation is part of analysis ¶ An analysis that nobody understands has no effect. The most important finding in a report can be lost in a cluttered table, a misleading chart or a slide with too much text. Good analysts therefore do three jobs: Find what is true in the data. docs.text: Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on.

Real stories where data changed the outcome

docs.text: During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows".
docs.title: A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854)

docs.text: After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it.
docs.title: A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s)

docs.text: The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money.
docs.title: Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002)

docs.text: Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions.
docs.title: Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004)

docs.text: Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation.

docs.text: How statistics can mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can support very different stories depending on how it is summarised, compared and drawn. Learn the common traps so you never fall into them, and can spot them in other people's work. In 1954, Darrell Huff wrote a short, famous book called How to Lie with Statistics . Its point was not to teach lying. It was to show readers how easily numbers mislead, often by accident. The traps below are the ones you will meet most often at work. 1. Correlation is not causation ¶ Two things that move together are correlated . That does not mean one causes the other. A classic example: in many cities, ice cream sales and crime both rise in summer and fall in winter. Plot one against the other and you see a strong relationship. Does ice cream cause crime? Of course not. Both are plausibly driven by a third factor, warm weather , when more people are outside. The chart uses synthetic data made up for illustration. The hidden third factor is called a confounder . Whenever you see two things moving together, ask: Could a third factor be driving both? Could the cause run the other way? Could it be coincidence, especially if I searched through many variables? Spurious correlations If you compare enough unrelated series, some will match by pure chance. Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations project collects amusing examples, such as films featuring a particular actor tracking the number of swimming-pool drownings in the same years. At work "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Perhaps the app made them spend more. Or perhaps the customers who already spent the most were the ones who bothered to download the app. Only a fair comparison or a test can tell you which. 2. Simpson's paradox: the total can reverse the parts ¶ In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley, looked at graduate admissions. Overall, 44% of men but only 35% of women were admitted. It looked like clear bias against women. But when the figures were split by department, the picture changed. The chart and table show the six largest departments; the overall row covers all departments. Department Men admitted Women admitted A 62% 82% B 63% 68% C 37% 34% D 33% 35% E 28% 24% F 6% 7% All departments (overall) 44% 35% What happened? Women applied mostly to departments that were very competitive for everyone (C to F). Men applied mostly to departments that admitted many applicants (A and B). The overall rate mixed together very different groups. The lesson Before comparing two overall rates, check whether the groups being compared have a different mix underneath. A total can tell the opposite story to every one of its parts. 3. Misleading axes ¶ The same two numbers can look dramatically different depending on where the axis starts. Synthetic data for illustration. Bar charts should start at zero, because we judge bars by their length. Line charts may start elsewhere, because we judge lines by their slope, but label the axis clearly. Watch for two different y-axes on one chart. They let the author make any two lines appear to move together. 4. Cherry-picked time windows ¶ Choose the start and end dates carefully and almost any trend can be made to look like growth or decline. "Sales up 40% since March!" (March was the worst month in five years.) "Complaints halved this quarter!" (Last quarter included a one-off system outage.) Synthetic data for illustration. The left chart is true, but the right chart shows the real story: March was an unusual low, and sales have been falling for five years. Ask Why does the chart start and end there ? What does the longer history look like? 5. Which average? ¶ The word "average" can mean different things: The mean adds everything up and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when everything is sorted. If a few values are extremely large, the mean is pulled upward. Imagine nine employees earning 40,000 and one director earning 1,000,000. The mean salary is 136,000; the median is 40,000. Both are "the average salary", but only one describes a typical employee. Synthetic data for illustration. Which to use Use the median for things with a few very large values, such as salaries, house prices or delivery delays. Report both when the difference matters. 6. Percentages without the base ¶ "Complaints rose 200%!" sounds alarming. From 1 to 3, it is not. From 10,000 to 30,000, it is a crisis. Synthetic data for illustration. Notice that the two charts look exactly the same. Only the axis numbers reveal how different the situations are. Always ask for the count behind a percentage. Be wary of averaging percentages from groups of very different sizes. You will meet this trap in the marketing case. 7. Survivorship bias ¶ As the story is usually told, during the Second World War analysts studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had been hit. The obvious idea was to add armour where the bullet holes were. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: these were the planes that survived . Planes hit in other places, such as the engines, never came back to be counted. The armour belonged where the returning planes had no holes. Simplified illustration, not real wartime data. At work Surveying only current customers about why they like you tells you nothing about why others left. Studying only successful projects hides the reasons projects fail. A checklist for any number you are shown ¶ Before you trust a figure, ask: Compared to what? A number without a comparison means little. Who or what is included? Which records, which dates, which filters? What is the denominator? Out of how many? Could something else explain it? A confounder, a different mix, chance? How is it drawn? Where does the axis start? Is the time window fair? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: name the confounder For each claim, suggest a third factor that could explain the link: Towns with more fire engines have more fire damage. Employees who attend more training get promoted more often. Stores with more staff have more customer complaints. Exercise 2: fix the chart Find a chart in a news article or a company report. Check where its axis starts, which time period it covers and whether the counts behind its percentages are shown. Rewrite its headline so it is fair. Exercise 3: spot the paradox A sales manager says: "Team A's overall conversion rate is lower than Team B's, so Team A is weaker." What extra breakdown would you ask for before agreeing?

docs.text: Statistics are not enough ¶ Averages, spreads and correlations are useful summaries. But very different data can produce exactly the same summary numbers. The only safe habit is to look at the data as well. Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe created four small datasets. Each has eleven points. Look at their summary statistics: Statistic Dataset I Dataset II Dataset III Dataset IV Mean of x 9.0 9.0 9.0 9.0 Mean of y 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50 Variance of x 11.0 11.0 11.0 11.0 Variance of y 4.13 4.13 4.12 4.12 Correlation of x and y 0.816 0.816 0.816 0.817 Best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x If you only read this table, you would say the four datasets are the same. Now look at them: Dataset What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing. This is the case the summary describes well. II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line at all. III A perfect straight line, except for one outlier A single unusual point drags the trend line. IV Almost all points share one x value; one extreme point creates the "trend" Remove that one point and every x is the same, so there is no trend left to measure. The lesson Summary statistics compress data. Compression throws information away. A chart lets you see what was thrown away. The raw data, if you want to plot it yourself x (I, II, III) y I y II y III x IV y IV 10 8.04 9.14 7.46 8 6.58 8 6.95 8.14 6.77 8 5.76 13 7.58 8.74 12.74 8 7.71 9 8.81 8.77 7.11 8 8.84 11 8.33 9.26 7.81 8 8.47 14 9.96 8.10 8.84 8 7.04 6 7.24 6.13 6.08 8 5.25 4 4.26 3.10 5.39 19 12.50 12 10.84 9.13 8.15 8 5.56 7 4.82 7.26 6.42 8 7.91 5 5.68 4.74 5.73 8 6.89 The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017, researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice took the idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawing made of data points (originally created by Alberto Cairo), they nudged points step by step into new shapes while keeping the summary statistics nearly identical, to about two decimal places. Every one of these thirteen datasets has: mean of x ≈ 54.3 and mean of y ≈ 47.8 standard deviation of x ≈ 16.8 and of y ≈ 26.9 correlation between x and y between −0.06 and −0.07 A report that said "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around 54 and 48" would be technically correct for all of them, including the dinosaur. Data source Datasaurus Dozen data from the open-source datasauRus package (MIT licence), based on Matejka and Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs , ACM CHI 2017. What this means at work ¶ You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. But you will meet the same problems in everyday forms: An average hides two very different groups. Average delivery time looks fine, because most deliveries are fast while a few customers wait weeks. One outlier drives the trend. A single huge order makes a quiet month look like growth. A relationship is curved, not straight. Discounts raise sales up to a point, then only cut profit. Rule of thumb Never report a summary number you have not also looked at in a chart, at least once, yourself. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: predict, then check Cover the Anscombe chart above. docs.text: Storytelling with data ¶ A correct analysis that nobody understands changes nothing. Storytelling with data means shaping evidence into a clear message, for a specific audience, that leads to a decision. The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation ¶ On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead. What did the data show? ¶ Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. Data source O-ring data for the 23 flights before Challenger: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Challenger USA Space Shuttle O-Ring dataset (erosion or blow-by version), based on Draper (1995) and Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989). What makes a data story ¶ The ideas in this section draw on Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's book Storytelling with Data (2015), paraphrased for this course. A data story is not a decorated chart. It has three parts: Context: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what decision do they face? Evidence: the few charts and numbers that matter, checked and clearly drawn. Action: what you recommend, what is uncertain, and how success will be measured. Start with the "big idea" ¶ Before building any chart, write your main message in one sentence that: states your point of view, says what is at stake, and is written for your audience. Example: "Delivery delays in the North region are costing us repeat customers, so we should trial a second carrier there next quarter before the peak season." If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to build the presentation. A simple process ¶ Know your audience. A finance director and a warehouse team need different levels of detail. Write the big idea in one sentence. Choose the right chart for each point (see Types of analysis ). Remove clutter (see Designing clear visuals ). Direct attention with one colour, a clear title and a short annotation. Build the flow: situation, complication, resolution. What is happening, why it is a problem, what we should do. Test it on someone who has not seen it. Can they repeat your message in one sentence? Titles that tell Replace descriptive titles with message titles. Instead of "Monthly sales by region" write "North region sales have fallen for three months while all others grew." Exploratory versus explanatory ¶ Exploratory Explanatory Purpose Find out what is in the data Tell others what you found Audience You Decision-makers Number of charts Many As few as possible Style Rough, quick Clean, titled, annotated Most of your time in analysis is exploratory. Only the few findings that matter make it into the explanatory story. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: rescue the Challenger chart Look at the left-hand Challenger chart. Write a one-sentence title for the right-hand chart that a manager could not misunderstand. Exercise 2: write a big idea Choose a recent finding from your own work, or from any chart on these Foundations pages. Write a big-idea sentence with a point of view, the stakes and the audience. Exercise 3: three slides, one story Plan a three-slide story about the ice cream and crime example on How statistics can mislead : Situation: what the raw correlation seems to say. Complication: what it hides. Resolution: what a decision-maker should do instead. Exercise 4: the one-sentence test Show any chart you have made to a colleague for ten seconds. Ask them what it says. docs.text: On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead.
docs.title: The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation

docs.text: Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. docs.text: Designing clear visuals ¶ A good chart lets the reader see the important comparison in seconds. That depends on removing what does not help, and on using what we know about how the eye and brain read pictures. The data-ink ratio ¶ Information designer Edward Tufte suggested a simple test. Of all the ink on a chart, how much actually shows data ? Everything else (heavy gridlines, borders, shading, 3D effects, decorative colours) is non-data ink. Tufte called unnecessary decoration chartjunk . Aim: increase the share of ink that carries data, without removing anything the reader needs. Synthetic data for illustration. What changed between the two versions: Removed the background shading, borders and hatching. Removed the gridlines and the value axis, and wrote the values directly on the bars. Sorted the bars, so the ranking is obvious. Used colour once , to point at the bar that matters. Turned the bars horizontal , so labels are easy to read. Do not overdo it Removing axis labels, units or context to make a chart "clean" makes it less useful. The goal is clarity, not minimalism. Pre-attentive attributes: what the eye sees first ¶ Some visual differences are noticed almost instantly, before we consciously think. These are called pre-attentive attributes . They include colour, size, position, orientation and boldness. Try it: count the number 3 in the top grid, then in the bottom grid. The bottom grid takes a second. The top one takes much longer. The only difference is one attribute: colour. Use this deliberately Make most of the chart grey, then use one strong colour or bold label for the thing you want the reader to see. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Gestalt principles: how we group things ¶ Our brains automatically group what we see. Designers use these Gestalt principles to make related items look related. Principle What it means Use it in a chart or dashboard Proximity Things close together seem related Put related charts next to each other; leave space between unrelated ones Similarity Things that look alike (colour, shape) seem related Use the same colour for the same category on every chart Enclosure Things inside a shared border or shaded area seem grouped Shade a time period, such as a promotion, on a line chart Connection Things joined by a line seem related Lines connect points in a time series; avoid lines between unrelated categories Closure We complete incomplete shapes in our minds Charts rarely need full borders; the eye fills them in Continuity We follow smooth paths Align charts and labels so the eye flows across the page Colour with purpose ¶ One colour for one meaning. If "East" is blue in one chart, keep it blue in every chart. Grey for context, colour for focus. Do not rely on colour alone. Around one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency. Add labels or patterns too. Avoid rainbow palettes for numbers. Use light-to-dark shades of one colour for "more" and "less". Avoid red and green as the only difference. It is the most common pair people cannot tell apart. A clean-chart checklist ¶ Does the title say what the reader should notice, not just what is plotted? Are axes labelled with units, and do bars start at zero? Is everything that is not data as light as possible? Is colour used only where it means something? Can someone who cannot see colour still read it? Would a sorted table or a single number be clearer than a chart? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: declutter Take a chart from a recent report at work, or any chart from the news. List every element that is not data. For each, decide: keep , lighten or remove . Sketch the improved version. Exercise 2: one highlight Sketch a bar chart of five products where only one product needs attention. Use grey for four bars and one colour for the fifth. Write a title that tells the reader what to notice. Exercise 3: spot the Gestalt Open any dashboard you use at work. Find one place where proximity or similarity helps you, and one place where it confuses you.

Predict before you run the next cell: will the number of rows equal the number of orders? print ( "Rows (order lines):" , len ( df )) print ( "Different orders: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Rows (order lines): 6815 Different orders: 3388 How many lines do orders usually have? groupby("order_id").size() counts the lines in each order; value_counts() then counts how many orders have 1 line, 2 lines, and so on. lines_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . size () . value_counts () . sort_index () lines_per_order . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "How many lines each order has, orders placed 2023–2025" ) plt . xlabel ( "Lines in the order" ) plt . ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () Many orders have one line, but plenty have several. That is why len(df) overstates the number of orders. Part 6: What the returns flag means ¶ returned_order_flag is 1 when an order is on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. The order you looked at in Part 5 is on the list. See how the flag repeats: df [ df [ "order_id" ] == "US-2023-100762" ][[ "row_id" , "order_id" , "returned_order_flag" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } row_id order_id returned_order_flag 1684 1685 US-2023-100762 1 1688 1689 US-2023-100762 1 1690 1691 US-2023-100762 1 1691 1692 US-2023-100762 1 Now compare two ways of counting: flagged = df [ df [ "returned_order_flag" ] == 1 ] print ( "Sum of the flag (counts LINES): " , df [ "returned_order_flag" ] . sum ()) print ( "Distinct orders on the returns list: " , flagged [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Sum of the flag (counts LINES): 511 Distinct orders on the returns list: 191 A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag counts lines of listed orders, not orders. To count orders on the returns list, filter to flag 1 and use nunique() on order_id , as in the second line of the output above. Say "orders on the returns list", not "returned orders" or "return rate": the list tells us membership only. That order is counted once in each category it touches, so the category counts add up to more than the overall total. Distinct counts do not always add up Sales and Profit can be added across groups. Distinct order counts can only be added when every order belongs to exactly one group. Always recount distinct orders at the level you display. The business decision ¶ The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. In this lesson you build a fair comparison. About the data The Superstore sample describes a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the currency is not stated, so never add a currency symbol. The source does not explain how Profit is calculated, so we say profit ratio , never "margin". What you will be able to do ¶ Define five measures precisely: Sales, Orders, Average order value, Profit and Profit ratio. Calculate them in pandas, for the whole table and for each segment. Calculate ratios from totals , not by averaging other ratios. Check that segment results reconcile with the overall total. Explain how a filter changes every measure. Write a short, evidence-based recommendation with one limitation. Evidence you keep: a segment KPI table, your metric definitions, a validation checklist and a five-sentence recommendation. Before you start, complete Lesson 2 and have your grain statement and evidence log ready. Re-read the averages and percentages traps in Foundations. Never average the ratios of individual rows or of segments. You will see why in Part 6. When there is nothing to divide by If a filter leaves no orders or no Sales, the ratio is not available . pandas shows this as NaN ("not a number"). Read it as "not available" , never as 0%. docs.text: Lesson 4: Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ¶ Add time to your segment comparison, read growth figures without being fooled by the seasons, use the returns list carefully, and bring it all together in one dashboard with a recommendation. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Build a monthly Sales trend and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Explain why a blank growth value means "no comparison", and why filtering too early creates blanks. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Combine three charts into one dashboard and write a recommendation for a test. Evidence you keep: your dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, and a five-sentence recommendation. Together they are your retail portfolio checkpoint . Before you start ¶ Complete Lesson 3 , where you built the segment KPI table. Re-read cherry-picked time windows and storytelling with data . About the data Superstore is a fictitious sample. Part 2: Two kinds of growth ¶ Growth type Compares each month with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous calendar month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month one year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Both use the same formula: (this month − comparison month) ÷ comparison month . Only on a complete monthly series pct_change compares each row with the row above it (or 12 rows above). That only means "previous month" or "same month last year" because we checked that all 36 months are present and in order. To see what is being compared, the table below also keeps the comparison values. shift(1) moves each value down one row; shift(12) moves it down twelve rows. growth = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : monthly }) growth [ "previous_month" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 1 ) growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change () growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 12 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) # A comparison month with zero Sales gives no fair growth figure: treat it as blank. growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "mom_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "previous_month" ] != 0 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "yoy_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] != 0 ) The full table has 36 rows. docs.text: Growth type Compares each month with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous calendar month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month one year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Both use the same formula: (this month − comparison month) ÷ comparison month . Only on a complete monthly series pct_change compares each row with the row above it (or 12 rows above). That only means "previous month" or "same month last year" because we checked that all 36 months are present and in order. To see what is being compared, the table below also keeps the comparison values. shift(1) moves each value down one row; shift(12) moves it down twelve rows. growth = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : monthly }) growth [ "previous_month" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 1 ) growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change () growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 12 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) # A comparison month with zero Sales gives no fair growth figure: treat it as blank. growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "mom_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "previous_month" ] != 0 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "yoy_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] != 0 ) The full table has 36 rows. docs.text: Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns-list share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison you would use to judge the test, such as YoY Sales for the same months, or the same months in a similar group that did not get the change. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A segment growing at the same time as something else happened is an association , not proof that one caused the other. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works.

Part 1: From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? docs.text: Tableau Lesson 2: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Before comparing anything, find out exactly what the retail file contains: what a row is, which columns can be added up, and how to count orders correctly. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Python Lesson 2 . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head now asks: "Before you show me any chart, can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" A wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today is about building trust in the data. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: State the grain of the file: what one row represents. Tell which columns are identifiers, categories, dates or amounts. Count orders correctly with a distinct count. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check a small slice of data by hand. Record what you changed in a short preparation log . Evidence you keep: a grain statement, a short quality checklist, a preparation log and one checked order. Before you start ¶ Bring your saved Lesson 1 workbook and your evidence log. Keep the original order_lines.csv untouched. If you ever need to experiment, work on a copy. Part 1: Meet the data dictionary ¶ Every column has a job. Knowing that job tells you how to use it. Column What it is Can you add it up? row_id Unique number for each order line No, it is an identifier order_id Order identifier; repeats across that order's lines No, count it distinctly order_date , ship_date Calendar dates No order_month First day of the order's month, for monthly grouping No ship_mode Shipping service chosen No customer_id Fictitious customer identifier No segment Customer group: Consumer, Corporate or Home Office No, use it to group country_region , region Location labels No, use them to group category , sub_category Product groups No, use them to group product_id , product_name Product identifier and name No sales Sales reported for the line, in the file's own monetary units Yes quantity Number of items on the line Yes , but it counts items, not orders profit Profit reported for the line (can be negative) Yes discount Discount value as given in the source No, its exact definition is not documented returned_order_flag 1 if the order appears on the source's returns list, otherwise 0 Not on line rows (see Part 4) order_to_ship_days Days between order date and ship date No, not without care customer_analysis_eligible , customer_order_conflict Flags for a small data issue with customer IDs Used only for customer analysis later Scope of this file The file contains orders placed from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025 . A few orders placed late in 2025 shipped in early 2026; they are kept because the order date is what defines the period. Part 2: Find the grain ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Open your workbook and go to the Data Source page. Sort or scan the preview by order_id . Find an order that appears on more than one row . Compare those rows. What is the same? What is different? Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in order_lines.csv represents one _ _ , identified by ____ ." Part 3: Count orders correctly ¶ Demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will show two numbers side by side: the number of rows (the field ending in (Count) ) the number of distinct orders Predict before you see them: will the two numbers be equal, or which will be larger? Guided practice ¶ On a new sheet, drag the (Count) field to the view. This counts rows. Drag Order Id into the view as well. Right-click it and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . This counts orders. Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ. A reusable calculation You can also create a calculated field named Orders with the formula: COUNTD([Order Id]) Use this whenever a chart needs a number of orders. Part 4: What the returns flag means ¶ returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag across lines counts lines of returned orders, not returned orders . To count returned orders, count distinct order_id values where the flag is 1. Part 5: Check one order by hand ¶ Pick one order with several lines. Filter the view to that single order_id . Show each line's sales and profit in a table. Add up the lines yourself on paper or in a spreadsheet. Compare with Tableau's total for that order. Do they match? Record the order ID, your hand total and Tableau's total in your log. Part 6: Keep a preparation log ¶ Write down every change you make to how the data is read or shaped, even small ones. Date What I changed Why How I checked it example Created calculated field Orders = COUNTD([Order Id]) Rows are order lines, not orders Compared with the row count; checked one order by hand The original file is never edited. Every change lives in Tableau or in your log. Part 7: Independent work ¶ For each Segment , build a small table showing: the number of rows, the number of distinct orders, total sales . Then answer in your log: Do the segment order counts add up to the overall order count? Why might that be true for Segment? Try the same with Category . Do category order counts add up to the overall total? Why not? Think about it Can one order contain products from more than one category? Can one order belong to more than one segment? Part 8: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends this summary: "We had [row count] orders, and [sum of returned_order_flag] of them were returned." Which two mistakes are in this sentence? What should each number be counting instead? How would you check your corrected numbers? Write your corrected sentence. You do not need to share the numbers with anyone yet. Exit ticket ¶ Your grain statement. Why rows and orders differ in this file. One thing the returns flag cannot tell you. After the lesson ¶ Finish the Segment and Category tables from Part 7. Complete your preparation log and one hand-checked order. Keep your workbook for Lesson 3 , where we compare segments using Sales, Profit and average order value.

docs.text: Grain means: what does one row represent? Open your workbook and go to the Data Source page. Sort or scan the preview by order_id . Find an order that appears on more than one row . Compare those rows. What is the same? What is different? Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in order_lines.csv represents one _ _ , identified by ____ ."

docs.text: Your facilitator will show two numbers side by side: the number of rows (the field ending in (Count) ) the number of distinct orders Predict before you see them: will the two numbers be equal, or which will be larger?
docs.title: Demonstration

docs.text: On a new sheet, drag the (Count) field to the view. This counts rows. Drag Order Id into the view as well. Right-click it and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . This counts orders. Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ. A reusable calculation You can also create a calculated field named Orders with the formula: COUNTD([Order Id]) Use this whenever a chart needs a number of orders.
docs.title: Guided practice

docs.text: returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag across lines counts lines of returned orders, not returned orders . To count returned orders, count distinct order_id values where the flag is 1.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 3: Which segment deserves a closer look? ¶ Compare the three customer segments using five measures, calculate each one correctly, check that the numbers add up, and make a careful recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Python Lesson 3 . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. Today you build a fair comparison. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Define five measures precisely: Sales, Orders, Average order value, Profit and Profit ratio. Build them in Tableau as calculated fields. Calculate ratios from totals , not by averaging other ratios. Check that segment results reconcile with the overall total. Explain how a filter changes every measure. Write a short, evidence-based recommendation with one limitation. Evidence you keep: a segment KPI table, your metric definitions, a validation checklist and a five-sentence recommendation. Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 2 , with the Orders calculated field. Have your grain statement and evidence log ready. Re-read the averages and percentages traps in Foundations. Part 1: Agree the measures ¶ Every measure uses the same rows : all order lines in the file, unless you deliberately apply a filter. Measure What it means How to calculate it Sales Total reported Sales Add up sales Orders Number of different orders Count distinct order_id Average order value (AOV) Typical Sales per order Sales ÷ Orders Profit Total reported Profit (can be negative) Add up profit Profit ratio Profit earned per unit of Sales Profit ÷ Sales About the money Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units. The currency is not stated, so do not add a currency symbol. The source does not explain exactly how Profit is calculated, so call it profit ratio , not "gross margin". Totals first, then divide AOV and Profit ratio must be calculated from the totals for whatever you are looking at. Never average the ratios of individual rows or of segments. You will see why in Part 6. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator builds the five measures for the whole file and shows them as a small table. Before each number appears, predict : Will AOV be larger or smaller than Sales divided by the number of rows ? Why? Can Profit ratio be negative? When? Part 3: Guided practice — build the calculations ¶ Create each calculated field ( Analysis → Create Calculated Field ). Type the name and formula exactly. Sales SUM([Sales]) Orders (from Lesson 2) COUNTD([Order Id]) AOV IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN SUM([Sales]) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Profit SUM([Profit]) Profit ratio IF SUM([Sales]) <> 0 THEN SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) END Why the IF? If a filter leaves no orders or no Sales, dividing would be undefined. The IF makes Tableau show a blank instead of an error or a misleading zero. A blank here means "not available" , never 0%. Format the results: Sales, Profit and AOV: number with two decimal places, no currency symbol. Profit ratio: percentage with one decimal place. Part 4: Guided practice — the segment table ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Segment to Rows . Drag Measure Names to Columns and Measure Values to the table area. Keep only your five measures. Turn on totals: Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Give the sheet a clear title, for example "Segment comparison, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units)" . Check that it reconciles ¶ Tick each check in your evidence log: The three segment Sales add up to the grand total. The three segment Profit values add up to the grand total. The three segment Orders add up to the grand total. (They should, because every order belongs to exactly one segment.) The grand total AOV equals total Sales ÷ total Orders. It is not the average of the three segment AOVs. The grand total Profit ratio equals total Profit ÷ total Sales. It is not the average of the three segment ratios. If a total looks wrong Check that every measure uses the same filters, and that the grand total is recalculated, not summed. Right-click the measure and check which aggregation the total uses. Part 5: Independent work ¶ A. Filter by region ¶ Duplicate your segment sheet. Add Region to Filters and choose one region. Record all five measures for each segment in that region. Write two sentences: does the ranking of segments change inside this region? B. Look at a category ¶ Duplicate the sheet again and filter to one Category . Notice that AOV now means "Sales of this category's lines per order that contains this category" , not full basket value. Rename the column to say so. Remove the filter and put Category on Rows instead of Segment. Do the category Orders add up to the overall total? Explain why not, in one sentence. Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends you this summary: "Our overall profit ratio is the average of the three segment ratios. And our average order value is total Sales divided by the number of rows." Calculate the colleague's two numbers from your own table. Compare them with your correct grand totals. Explain each mistake in one sentence. Which segment has the most influence on the correct overall profit ratio, and why? Think about weights A segment with much more Sales should pull the overall ratio more strongly than a small segment. Does a simple average of the three ratios allow that? Part 7: Make a recommendation ¶ Write five sentences to the retail head: Recommendation: which segment to investigate first. Evidence 1: one measure, with its value and how it compares. Evidence 2: a second, different measure. Limitation: one thing this data cannot tell you. For example, it shows which segment looks different; it does not show why , and it does not prove a discount or promotion caused anything. Next check: one specific piece of evidence to request before changing promotions. Association, not cause If a segment with more discounts has a lower profit ratio, that is a pattern worth investigating. It is not proof that the discounts caused it. Other differences between segments, such as product mix, could explain it. Validation checklist ¶ Before submitting, confirm: Every measure uses the same filters and date scope. Orders are counted distinctly, not as rows. AOV and Profit ratio are calculated from totals. Segment Sales, Profit and Orders reconcile with the grand totals. Money is labelled "source monetary units", with no currency symbol. The recommendation names a limitation and a next check. Exit ticket ¶ Why is the average of three segment ratios not the overall ratio? What does a blank AOV or Profit ratio mean? One question you would want answered before acting on your recommendation. After the lesson ¶ Finish the region and category work from Part 5. Correct the colleague's summary in Part 6 and add it to your evidence log. Keep your workbook for Lesson 4 , where we look at monthly trends and the returns list, and build a dashboard.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 4: Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ¶ Add time to your segment comparison, read growth figures without being fooled by seasons, use the returns list carefully, and bring it all together in one dashboard with a recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Python Lesson 4 . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Build a monthly Sales trend and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Combine views into a dashboard with one shared filter. Write a recommendation for a test, with an honest limitation. Evidence you keep: a retail dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, and a short recommendation. This dashboard is your retail portfolio checkpoint . Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 3 with the segment KPI table. Re-read cherry-picked time windows and storytelling with data . Part 1: The monthly trend ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Order Month to Columns . Right-click it and choose the continuous Month option (green pill), so every month from January 2023 to December 2025 appears in order. Drag your Sales measure to Rows . You now have a line chart. Add Segment to Color to see one line per segment. Then remove it again for the overall view. What do you notice? Write down three observations. Look at the same months in different years. Are some months always high? Are January and February always low? Use the month field order_month is the first day of each order's month. Using it keeps every order in the right calendar month and makes year-on-year comparisons simple. Part 2: Two kinds of growth ¶ Month-on-month growth ¶ Compares each month with the previous month. IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) END Year-on-year growth ¶ Compares each month with the same month one year earlier . IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) END To use them: Create both as calculated fields and format them as percentages with one decimal place. Put Order Month (continuous month) on Columns and one growth measure on Rows. Right-click the growth measure, choose Compute Using , and select Order Month . Blank is correct sometimes January 2023 has no previous month in this file, so its month-on-month growth is blank. All of 2023 has no year-earlier month, so its year-on-year growth is blank. Blank means "no comparison available" , never 0%. Filters can remove the comparison LOOKUP compares with the previous month shown in the view . If you filter the view to only 2025, January 2025 can no longer see December 2024 and becomes blank. Keep all months in the view and highlight the period you care about instead of filtering it away. Which one is fair? ¶ Growth type Good for Can mislead when Month-on-month Spotting sudden changes The business is seasonal: January after a busy December always looks like a crash Year-on-year Comparing like with like across seasons A one-off event happened in the same month last year Part 3: The returns list ¶ From Lesson 2, you know the returns flag marks orders that appear on the source's returns list . Create two measures: Orders on returns list COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) Share of orders on returns list IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Add the share to your segment table. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it. A separate synthetic exercise will cover refund amounts later. Part 4: Guided practice — build the dashboard ¶ Create a new dashboard ( Dashboard → New Dashboard ). Drag in three sheets: your segment KPI table from Lesson 3, with the returns share added the monthly Sales trend the year-on-year growth chart Add a Region filter. Click its menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source , so every view responds together. Give each sheet a message title that says what to notice, for example in the form "[Segment] sales [rose / fell] most in [period]" , filled in with what your chart actually shows. Add one short text box stating the scope: "Orders placed 2023–2025. Source monetary units. Fictitious sample data." Design checks ¶ Use what you learned in Designing clear visuals : The most important view is at the top left. Colour is used only where it means something, and each segment keeps the same colour everywhere. Every chart has labelled axes with units. Nothing can be understood only by colour; labels or a table are available too. When you change the Region filter, all views change together and the totals still reconcile. Part 5: Independent work ¶ Choose one segment . Using your dashboard, describe its trend over the three years in three sentences. Compare the same quarter across years for that segment. Is it growing, flat or falling? Add one annotation to the trend chart marking something a manager should notice ( right-click a point → Annotate → Mark ). Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague posts this in a team chat: "Disaster! Sales fell about 75% in January 2025. And I filtered the dashboard to 2025 to check, but now January's growth is blank. Something is broken." Is January's fall a real problem, or a seasonal pattern? Which growth measure would you show instead, and what does it say? Why did January's month-on-month growth become blank after filtering to 2025? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate. Part 7: Recommend a test ¶ Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison period you would use to judge the test, such as year-on-year Sales and profit ratio for the same months. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works. Validation checklist ¶ The trend shows all 36 months with no gaps. Growth measures compute along Order Month, and blanks appear only where no comparison exists. Returns are counted as distinct orders, not lines. The dashboard filter changes every view, and segment totals still reconcile with the overall total. Titles state messages; scope and units are written on the dashboard. Exit ticket ¶ Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What is one thing the returns list cannot tell you? What would you measure to judge whether your proposed test worked? After the lesson ¶ Finish your dashboard and recommendation. Together they form your retail portfolio checkpoint . Save the workbook locally with a clear name, and record the file name in your evidence log.

Is it growing, flat or falling? Add one annotation to the trend chart marking something a manager should notice ( right-click a point → Annotate → Mark ).
docs.title: Part 5: Independent work

docs.text: A colleague posts this in a team chat: "Disaster! Sales fell about 75% in January 2025. And I filtered the dashboard to 2025 to check, but now January's growth is blank. Something is broken." Is January's fall a real problem, or a seasonal pattern? Which growth measure would you show instead, and what does it say? Why did January's month-on-month growth become blank after filtering to 2025? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate.
docs.title: Part 6: Debugging challenge

docs.text: Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison period you would use to judge the test, such as year-on-year Sales and profit ratio for the same months. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works.
docs.title: Part 7: Recommend a test

docs.text: The trend shows all 36 months with no gaps. Growth measures compute along Order Month, and blanks appear only where no comparison exists. Returns are counted as distinct orders, not lines. The dashboard filter changes every view, and segment totals still reconcile with the overall total. Titles state messages; scope and units are written on the dashboard.
docs.title: Validation checklist

docs.text: Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What is one thing the returns list cannot tell you? What would you measure to judge whether your proposed test worked?
docs.title: Exit ticket

docs.text: Finish your dashboard and recommendation. Together they form your retail portfolio checkpoint . Save the workbook locally with a clear name, and record the file name in your evidence log.
